617.title: Mud and spit (John 9:1–12)
617.hook: who sinned, this man or his parents? neither; he makes clay and says go wash
617.howItsDone: Christians often read this chapter in Lent, and many churches connect the washing in Siloam with baptism, which early Christians sometimes called illumination.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a famous sentence and the quieter one before it: if ye continue in my word. Your line was the truth shall make you free.

When something terrible happens, people reach for a reason. A diagnosis, an accident, a child born with a disability, and the question comes, out loud or whispered: what did they do to deserve this? It's an old question. Jesus and his friends pass a man who has been blind since birth, and the disciples, without even lowering their voices, turn him into a theology problem. "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" The man can hear them.

The disciples give Jesus two choices, and he refuses both. "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Neither. The blindness isn't a punishment. Christians have wrestled with the second half of that verse. Does it mean God made him blind just to make a point? Some readers answer by moving the full stop: neither this man sinned nor his parents. Period. Then: so that the works of God may be shown, we must work while it is day. Read that way, Jesus doesn't explain the blindness. He moves straight from blame to work. Then he does something earthy: "he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay." Not a word from a distance this time, like with the official's son. Touch. Some early Christian writers saw an echo of Genesis, where God forms the first human from the dust of the ground. Then: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.)" The man has to walk there still blind, mud on his face, through the streets of Jerusalem. "He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing." And the pool is real: workers repairing a pipe in Jerusalem uncovered stone steps of a large pool from Jesus's time, which archaeologists identify as Siloam.
screen: `MUD AND SPIT, LIKE DUST IN EDEN.`
then, large: `NEITHER HATH THIS MAN SINNED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who is suffering, a friend, a stranger in the news, maybe yourself, and notice any quiet explanation in you: they should have known, they brought it on themselves, I must deserve this. Don't argue with it; just notice it and set it down, then ask the question Jesus moved to instead: what work could I do here? If you pray, hold that person before God without explanations; if you don't, just hold them with care.
Siloam. The pool where Jesus sent a man born blind to wash off the clay, which John says means Sent.
Your line: neither sinned. The blame stops there, and the work begins. See you tomorrow.

618.title: Now I see (John 9:13–41)
618.hook: the healed man is questioned, thrown out, and found again by Jesus
618.howItsDone: Christians often share testimonies, simple accounts of what God has done in their lives, and the healed man's "one thing I know" is a common model; the hymn Amazing Grace echoes his words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mud and spit, and a walk to the pool called Siloam, which means Sent. Your line was neither sinned.

A miracle ought to end in a party. A man blind from birth can see. Instead, chapter nine becomes a courtroom drama. The neighbors argue about whether it's even him: some say yes, others say no, he just looks like him. And the man keeps saying, I am he. Then he's brought to the religious leaders, and the questions start. How did this happen? Who did it? On the sabbath? The man who was blind is about to be questioned three times, and he gets braver each time.

The first time, he just tells the facts: he put clay on my eyes, I washed, and I see. The leaders are divided. Some say a man who heals on the sabbath can't be from God. Others ask how a sinner could do such signs. What do you think? He's a prophet, the man says. Then they call his parents, who, frightened, say only: this is our son, and he was born blind. How he sees, we don't know. Ask him; he's of age. John says they were afraid of being put out of the synagogue. Some readers think this detail also reflects John's own time, when followers of Jesus and other Jewish communities were painfully parting ways. The man is called back and pressed: we know this man is a sinner. He answers: "whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." He doesn't try to win the theology argument. He stands on the one thing he's sure of. Then he even gets cheeky: why hear it again? Will ye also be his disciples? And they throw him out. Here's the turn: "Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him," he asks: do you believe in the Son of man? Who is he, Lord? You've seen him; he's talking with you. "Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him." Thrown out by one door, he's found by the one who came looking.
screen: then, large: `WHEREAS I WAS BLIND, NOW I SEE.`

segments.voice: Let the big questions you can't answer be there, unresolved: about God, about suffering, about what happens next. Then find one thing you know from your own life, a time you were helped, a change in you, a moment of beauty you can't explain away, and hold it simply, without arguing for it. If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, let it be solid ground.
Synagogue. What the healed man's parents feared being cast out of, for saying too much about who healed him.
Your line: one thing I know. You don't need every answer to say it. Day six hundred eighteen.

619.title: I am the gate (John 10:1–10)
619.hook: I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly
619.howItsDone: Christians often quote John 10:10 when describing the life they hope faith brings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man questioned three times, thrown out, and found again, and the word synagogue. Your line was one thing I know.

A sheepfold on a hillside: a rough circle of stone walls, chest high, with one gap for an opening. At night the sheep are led inside, safe from wolves and thieves. Jesus is still talking to the listeners who threw the healed man out. He tells them a picture-story: sheep, a gatekeeper, thieves who climb over the wall, and a shepherd who walks in through the door. John says plainly they didn't understand it. So Jesus tries again, more directly.

First, the shepherd. The sheep hear his voice, and "he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." Not a herd. Names. Then the surprise: "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture." The King James says door; some modern Bibles say gate. Either way, it's the opening in the wall. John has given us I am sayings before: bread, light. Now, the way in. People often tell how a shepherd in that region might lie down across the gap at night, so nothing could get in or out without stepping over him. Whether or not every shepherd did that, it's a good picture of what Jesus is saying. And look at the words: go in and out. A gate isn't only for locking in. In, to rest at night. Out, to pasture in the morning. Then the verse behind today's line: "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly." The Greek word behind abundantly means more than enough, overflowing. Not just getting by. Life with something left over. Christians often hold this line as a picture of what faith is meant to be: not a smaller life fenced in by rules, but a bigger one, with a safe place to come home to.

Think of your day as it's going to go, how much of it is errands, emails, just getting through; that's real, and it's fine. Now picture one small thing that's more than necessary, a longer walk, a real conversation, cooking something properly, ten minutes outside, music you love played loud, and choose one. If you pray, give thanks for the life you have and ask for it in full; if not, just savor the thing you chose.
Sheepfold. The walled hillside pen Jesus pictures, with one gap for a gate: the shepherd leads his sheep in to rest, and out to pasture.
Your line: life to the full. In to rest, out to pasture. See you tomorrow.

620.title: The good shepherd (John 10:11–18)
620.hook: he knows his sheep and lays down his life
620.howItsDone: Many churches keep a Good Shepherd Sunday in the Easter season, and the image of Christ carrying a sheep remains common in stained glass, children's Bibles and church art.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sheepfold with one gap in the wall, and Jesus saying: I am the door. Your line was life to the full.

Go down into the catacombs under Rome, the underground burial passages of the early Christians, and look at the painted walls. Long before the cross became the most common Christian image, one picture shows up again and again: a young man with a sheep across his shoulders, holding its legs in front of his chest. Some of these paintings go back to the two hundreds, the third century. When the first Christians wanted to picture Jesus near the graves of the people they loved, many of them chose this. It comes from today's words.

"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." This is the fourth I am saying in John, right on the heels of the door. The word for good is kalos: good, and also beautiful, noble. The shepherd as he ought to be. Jesus sets him beside the hired hand. The hireling, as the King James calls him, sees a wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and runs. Not because he's evil. Because they're not his sheep; he's paid by the day. The good shepherd stays, because they're his own. Then a line of real tenderness: "I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine." Knowing goes both ways. Shepherd pictures run deep in the scriptures Jesus grew up with. King David was a shepherd. Psalm twenty-three begins, the Lord is my shepherd. In Ezekiel, God condemns shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock, and promises to search for the lost sheep himself. Jesus steps into that old picture, and adds: "And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold." Christians have long read that as a sign the flock would grow wider than anyone listening expected. And the most striking part: no one takes his life from him. "I lay it down of myself." The good shepherd isn't caught off guard. He chooses to give his life for the sheep, freely.
screen: then, large: `I LAY IT DOWN OF MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Think of the people you see often but don't really know, the person at the coffee shop, a neighbor, someone at work you nod to, and pick one whose name you know or would like to learn, and picture saying it to them warmly. Then remember a time someone used your name when you didn't expect them to know it, and how that felt. If you pray, give thanks that you're known by name; if not, just hold the feeling of being known.

Your line: I know my own. The good shepherd stays when the wolf comes. That's day six hundred twenty.

621.title: At the feast of Dedication (John 10:22–42)
621.hook: in winter, at Hanukkah in Solomon's porch, they ask him plainly
621.howItsDone: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight nights each winter, lighting one more light each night; Christians read this passage as Jesus's plain claim of unity with the Father and a promise that his own are held safe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a painting in the catacombs, and the good shepherd who stays when the hireling runs. Your line was I know my own.

"And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter." Two little facts, and they set a whole scene. The feast of the dedication is Hanukkah, whose own story is told in First Maccabees, a book that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include. And it's winter, cold enough that Jesus is walking under cover, in the colonnade called Solomon's porch. A crowd gathers close around him there, maybe blocking his way, and asks the question that has followed him for chapters.

First, the feast. Long before Jesus, a Greek king named Antiochus the Fourth set up pagan worship in the temple in Jerusalem and tried to stamp out Jewish practice. A family called the Maccabees led a revolt. When they took back the temple, they cleansed it and dedicated it again, with an eight-day celebration. Hanukkah means dedication. The famous story of a small jar of oil burning for eight days is told later, in the Talmud. Jews keep Hanukkah to this day, lighting lights in winter. So here is Jesus, at the feast that remembers the temple made holy again. The crowd says: "How long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly." His answer: I've told you, and the works I do tell you. My sheep hear my voice. Then a promise: "And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." Pluck is the King James word; some modern Bibles say snatch, like a wolf grabbing a lamb. And no one can pluck them out of my Father's hand, either. "I and my Father are one." The crowd hears it as blasphemy and picks up stones again. He escapes across the Jordan, to the place where John baptized at the very start, and there, John says, many believed. The story circles back to where it began.
screen: then, large: `I AND MY FATHER ARE ONE.`

segments.voice: If there's a candle or lamp nearby, light it or switch it on; if not, picture one, and watch the light for a moment. Think of someone going through a winter right now, grief, illness, loneliness, fear, and picture them held safe in hands that won't let go, and yourself too, if you're in a winter of your own. If you pray, hold them in the promise that no one can snatch them away; if not, simply keep the light company.

622.title: I am the resurrection (John 11:1–27)
622.hook: Martha meets him on the road and makes her confession
622.carry: though he were dead, yet shall he live
622.howItsDone: Jesus's words to Martha are often read at Christian funerals; in the Book of Common Prayer burial service, they are the first words said as the body is brought to the church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hanukkah in winter, under Solomon's porch, and hands that won't let go. Your line was no one can snatch them.

A message arrives across the Jordan from two sisters in Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem. It's short, and it doesn't ask for anything directly: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Their brother Lazarus. John adds, so we can't miss it: "Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus." And then the strangest sentence. Right after telling us he loved them, John says that when Jesus heard Lazarus was sick, he stayed where he was two more days. John doesn't explain the wait. Not yet.

When Jesus finally says, let's go back to Judea, the disciples are alarmed: they tried to stone you there. Thomas, the one later remembered for doubting, says something brave and bleak: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." By the time they reach Bethany, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days, and friends have come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters. Martha, hearing Jesus is near, doesn't wait at home. She goes out to meet him on the road. Her first words are honest, almost an accusation: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Then, in the same breath, she says she knows God will give him whatever he asks. Jesus says: your brother will rise again. Martha answers with a hope she already holds: "I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Someday. Far off. And Jesus brings it into the present tense: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Not, there will be a resurrection. I am. Then he asks her: believest thou this? And Martha makes her confession: "Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world." In Matthew's Gospel, it's Peter who says something like this. In John, it's Martha, grieving on a road, her brother four days in the tomb.
screen: then, large: `I AM THE RESURRECTION, AND THE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Martha said two things in one breath: if you had been here, and I believe; grief and faith together. Find one sentence that's true for you today, about God, or something simpler: that love matters, that people can change, that the person you lost still matters, and quietly say it out loud. If you pray, say it to God, the way Martha did; if not, say it to the room.

623.title: Jesus wept (John 11:28–44)
623.hook: he weeps with Mary, then calls Lazarus out and says: unbind him
623.howItsDone: Christians often turn to "Jesus wept" in times of grief, as a sign that mourning is not a failure of faith; the raising of Lazarus is read in some churches in Lent, and the Orthodox Church keeps Lazarus Saturday before Palm Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha on the road, and Jesus saying: I am the resurrection, and the life. Your line was though he were dead, yet shall he live.
screen: `THOUGH HE WERE DEAD, YET SHALL HE LIVE.`

segments.voice: Martha goes home and whispers to her sister: the Master is here, and he's asking for you. Mary gets up quickly and goes out. The mourners follow her, thinking she's going to the tomb to weep there. She finds Jesus, falls at his feet, and says exactly what her sister said: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Same sentence, different sister. But this time Jesus doesn't answer with a teaching. No I am. No question. He looks at her, crying, and at the people crying with her.

John says "he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled." The Greek word for groaned is strong, almost angry, a deep shudder. He asks where they've laid him. Come and see, they say, the words Jesus once used to his first disciples, now leading him to a grave. And then: "Jesus wept." Two words in the King James Bible, and a whole verse. He knows what he's about to do. He's just told Martha, I am the resurrection. And he weeps anyway. John lets grief and faith stand side by side. The people watching say: "Behold how he loved him!" At the tomb, a cave with a stone across it, he says, take away the stone. Martha, practical to the end, objects: "Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days." Jesus prays aloud, then cries with a loud voice: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man comes out, still wrapped hand and foot in grave clothes, his face bound with a cloth. Then the last command: "Loose him, and let him go." Notice who does the unbinding. Not Jesus. The people standing around. Jesus calls Lazarus to life; the community unwraps him. This week we've walked a long way: Siloam, synagogue, the door, hireling, Hanukkah in winter, Martha on the road, and now tears at a tomb, and a man walking out of it.
screen: then, large: `LOOSE HIM, AND LET HIM GO.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who has come through something hard, an illness, a loss, an addiction, a bad season, but is still wrapped in the old cloths: loneliness, shame, a debt or practical problem, other people's memories of who they were. Ask what small part of that you could help loosen: a ride, a meal, an invitation, forgetting the old story. If you pray, hold them before God; if not, hold them in mind kindly.
Jesus wept. Two words in the King James Bible: Jesus weeping with Mary at his friend's grave, moments before calling him out.
Your line: loose him, let him go. Another week on the path, and a good one to end on.
